archetype_description: Jeremiah is the most striking case in the Hebrew Bible of two divergent literary editions preserved in the textual record: a shorter, earlier edition (reflected in the Old Greek and 4QJer-b,d) and a longer, expanded edition (reflected in MT and 4QJer-a,c) that is roughly one-eighth longer and orders the Oracles Against the Nations differently. The compositional core derives from the prophet's own oracles (late 7th–early 6th c. BCE) transmitted via Baruch ben Neriah, with subsequent Deuteronomistic redaction during and after the exile. Tov, Janzen, and Stipp have argued that the Greek Vorlage represents an earlier Hebrew edition, while the proto-MT represents a secondary expansion.

stemma_nodes.label: Proto-Text (Jeremianic Oracles)
stemma_nodes.description: Original oracles of Jeremiah, partly dictated to Baruch (cf. Jer 36).

stemma_nodes.label: Deuteronomistic Redaction
stemma_nodes.description: Exilic Deuteronomistic editorial layer shaping the prose sermons and biographical narratives.

stemma_nodes.label: Short Hebrew Edition (Edition I)
stemma_nodes.description: Earlier, shorter Hebrew recension underlying the Old Greek and 4QJer-b,d.

stemma_nodes.label: Long Hebrew Edition (Edition II) / proto-MT
stemma_nodes.description: Expanded Hebrew edition with rearranged Oracles Against the Nations, ancestor of MT and 4QJer-a,c.

stemma_nodes.label: 4QJer-a (4Q70)
stemma_nodes.description: Qumran scroll aligning with proto-MT long edition.

stemma_nodes.label: 4QJer-c (4Q72)
stemma_nodes.description: Qumran fragment aligning with proto-MT.

stemma_nodes.label: 4QJer-b (4Q71)
stemma_nodes.description: Small Qumran fragment of Jer 9–10 in short form, agreeing with LXX Vorlage.

stemma_nodes.label: 4QJer-d (4Q72a)
stemma_nodes.description: Fragment of Jer 43 in short form, agreeing with LXX Vorlage.

stemma_nodes.label: Proto-MT (consonantal)
stemma_nodes.description: Stabilized consonantal text adopted by rabbinic Judaism.

stemma_nodes.label: MT
stemma_nodes.description: Tiberian Masoretic vocalization and accentuation tradition for Jeremiah.

stemma_nodes.label: Aleppo Codex
stemma_nodes.description: Ben-Asher model codex; Jeremiah is largely preserved.

stemma_nodes.label: Leningrad Codex (B19A)
stemma_nodes.description: Oldest complete Hebrew Bible, base text of BHS/BHQ.

stemma_nodes.label: BHS
stemma_nodes.description: Diplomatic edition of Leningrad with critical apparatus.

stemma_nodes.label: BHQ Jeremiah
stemma_nodes.description: Fifth edition with full Masorah and revised apparatus (Jeremiah fascicle by R. D. Weis).

stemma_nodes.label: Old Greek Jeremiah
stemma_nodes.description: Original Greek translation of the short Hebrew edition, made in Alexandria.

stemma_nodes.label: LXX Jeremiah
stemma_nodes.description: Greek tradition reflecting the short edition; ch. 46–51 MT correspond to LXX 25–31.

stemma_nodes.label: kaige section (Jer 29–52 LXX = MT 47–51 etc.)
stemma_nodes.description: Tov demonstrated that Jer-β (LXX Jer 29ff.) is a kaige-style revision toward a proto-MT Hebrew.

stemma_nodes.label: Origen's Hexapla
stemma_nodes.description: Origen's fifth column with asterisks marking pluses from MT brought into the LXX.

stemma_nodes.label: Lucianic (Antiochene) Recension
stemma_nodes.description: Antiochene revision preserving some pre-Hexaplaric Old Greek readings.

stemma_nodes.label: Aquila
stemma_nodes.description: Hyper-literal translation of proto-MT Jeremiah, preserved in fragments.

stemma_nodes.label: Symmachus
stemma_nodes.description: Idiomatic Greek revision toward proto-MT, preserved in fragments and Hexapla.

stemma_nodes.label: Codex Vaticanus (B)
stemma_nodes.description: Major uncial witness to LXX Jeremiah, relatively free of Hexaplaric contamination.

stemma_nodes.label: Codex Sinaiticus (S)
stemma_nodes.description: Major uncial witness to LXX Jeremiah.

stemma_nodes.label: Codex Alexandrinus (A)
stemma_nodes.description: Uncial with Hexaplaric influence in Jeremiah.

stemma_nodes.label: Göttingen Jeremiah (Ziegler)
stemma_nodes.full_name: Septuaginta: Vetus Testamentum Graecum XV: Ieremias
stemma_nodes.description: Joseph Ziegler's critical eclectic edition of LXX Jeremiah, Baruch, Lamentations, Epistle of Jeremiah.

stemma_nodes.label: NETS Jeremiah
stemma_nodes.full_name: New English Translation of the Septuagint, Jeremiah
stemma_nodes.description: English translation of Ziegler's Göttingen text by A. Pietersma and M. Saunders.

stemma_nodes.label: Peshitta Jeremiah
stemma_nodes.description: Syriac translation made from a proto-MT Hebrew Vorlage with occasional LXX influence.

stemma_nodes.label: Leiden Peshitta
stemma_nodes.full_name: The Old Testament in Syriac (Peshitta Institute, Leiden)
stemma_nodes.description: Critical edition of Peshitta Jeremiah.

stemma_nodes.label: Targum Jonathan to the Prophets
stemma_nodes.description: Official rabbinic Aramaic translation of the Prophets, based on proto-MT, with interpretive expansions.

stemma_nodes.label: Vulgate Jeremiah
stemma_nodes.description: Jerome's translation iuxta Hebraeos from a proto-MT Hebrew text, reflecting the long edition; ordering and verse numbering follow MT.

stemma_nodes.label: Stuttgart Vulgate
stemma_nodes.description: Weber-Gryson critical edition of the Vulgate.

key_divergences.title: Length difference: LXX one-eighth shorter than MT
key_divergences.plain: The Greek version of Jeremiah is roughly 13% shorter than the Hebrew, lacking thousands of words. This is not random loss but reflects two genuinely different editions of the book that circulated in antiquity.
key_divergences.technical: J. G. Janzen (1973) and E. Tov demonstrated that LXX reflects an earlier, shorter Hebrew Vorlage (Edition I), while MT reflects a later expansionist edition (Edition II) characterized by titles, double-readings, and explicating pluses. 4QJer-b,d confirm a Hebrew Vorlage close to LXX.

key_divergences.title: Placement of Oracles Against the Nations
key_divergences.plain: The oracles against foreign nations stand in the middle of the LXX (after 25:13) but at the end of the MT, and the nations are listed in different orders. This shows the book was reorganized at some stage of its transmission.
key_divergences.technical: LXX places OAN after Jer 25:13 in a sequence Elam-Egypt-Babylon-Philistia-Edom-Ammon-Kedar-Damascus-Moab; MT relocates them to chs. 46–51 with Egypt first and Babylon climactically last. Tov, Stipp, and Bogaert regard the MT arrangement as secondary, an editorial repositioning to give Babylon eschatological emphasis.

key_divergences.title: The shorter form of Jeremiah 10:6–8, 10
key_divergences.plain: The MT polemic against idols in Jer 10 is several verses longer than in the LXX, and 4QJer-b confirms the shorter Hebrew form. This is one of the clearest small-scale proofs that MT expanded an earlier text.
key_divergences.technical: LXX and 4QJer-b (4Q71) lack vv. 6–8 and 10 and order v. 9 within v. 5; the MT pluses are doxological expansions in late biblical Hebrew style. Cross, Tov, and E. Ulrich treat 4QJer-b as decisive corroboration that the LXX Vorlage is genuinely Hebrew rather than a translator's abbreviation.

key_divergences.title: kaige revision in the second half of LXX Jeremiah
key_divergences.plain: The second half of Greek Jeremiah translates Hebrew differently from the first half, suggesting either two translators or a later reviser bringing the Greek into closer agreement with a Hebrew text like the MT.
key_divergences.technical: H. St. J. Thackeray first noted the bisection (Jer-α, Jer-β); Tov (1976) reinterpreted Jer-β as a kaige-style revision of the Old Greek toward proto-MT, evidenced by characteristic equivalents (e.g., אנכי = ἐγώ εἰμι). This complicates use of LXX Jer 29–52 as a witness to the short edition.

key_divergences.title: Divergent endings: Jeremiah 52 and the historical appendix
key_divergences.plain: The colophon at 51:64 ('thus far the words of Jeremiah') signals the original ending, with chapter 52 being a later historical appendix borrowed from 2 Kings. Both LXX and MT preserve this appendix but with significant differences.
key_divergences.technical: Jer 52 is a secondary addition paralleling 2 Kgs 24:18–25:30, and LXX lacks Jer 52:28–30 (the deportation statistics). Bogaert and Stipp argue this confirms the editorial layering of the book's conclusion across both editions.

transmission_narrative: Jeremiah's transmission history is the textbook case of pluriformity in late Second Temple Judaism: two distinct Hebrew editions—a shorter one (Edition I) underlying the Old Greek and 4QJer-b,d, and a longer, rearranged one (Edition II) underlying MT and 4QJer-a,c—coexisted in Palestine until the proto-MT achieved hegemony around the turn of the era. The Old Greek was produced in Alexandria in the mid-2nd century BCE from Edition I, but its second half (Jer-β) was already revised toward proto-MT in a kaige-style recension before Origen further harmonized the Greek to the Hebrew in the Hexapla, with downstream effects in the Lucianic recension and in Codex Alexandrinus. Jerome's Vulgate (c. 392 CE) translated the long edition iuxta Hebraeos, fixing MT's chapter order in Western Christianity, while Targum Jonathan and the Peshitta likewise depend on proto-MT. Modern critical scholarship (Janzen, Tov, Stipp, Bogaert, Weis) has reached broad consensus that LXX Jeremiah is not a free translation but a faithful witness to an older Hebrew form, making Jeremiah the strongest exemplar of multiple literary editions within the Hebrew Bible.
transmission_plain: The book of Jeremiah survives in two genuinely different ancient editions: a shorter, older one preserved in Greek and a couple of Dead Sea Scrolls, and a longer, rearranged one that became the Hebrew Bible used today. Both versions are real and ancient—neither is a mistake—and together they let us watch a biblical book grow and be reorganized over centuries. Modern scholars use the Hebrew Masoretic manuscripts (especially the Leningrad Codex of 1008 CE) and the Greek Septuagint side by side to recover this layered history.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Two ancient editions of one biblical book
bibcrit_assessment.plain: Jeremiah is the clearest proof in the Hebrew Bible that scripture circulated in multiple authoritative editions before the text was standardized, and the Dead Sea Scrolls confirmed it by preserving Hebrew copies of both forms.
